newsitem.title: BRAZIL: YEAREND - Brazil reforms seen hinging on re-election.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Brazil reforms seen hinging on re-election.

text.p: If 1996 was the year when the Brazilian government's flagship reforms of the state ground to a halt, then 1997 may prove a year of progress with re-election acting as the catalyst, analysts and deputies said.
A constitutional amendment giving President Fernando Henrique Cardoso the chance to run in the 1998 presidential elections is expected to be put to a first vote in the Chamber of Deputies in January.
Approval of re-election is far from guaranteed because the government needs two successive three-fifths majority votes in the notoriously volatile lower house.

But even the opposition agrees the prospect of six more Cardoso years, as opposed to the current two remaining in his present term, would galvanize Congress behind the president and his drive to streamline the state.

"If he gets the chance of re-election, the president will be a very powerful force," said Marcello Deda, a deputy with the left-wing Workers Party (PT), which opposes re-election. "If he loses, then he's dead and buried as a president."

The deputy conceded, however, that the government probably had enough muscle to get the 308 votes it needs twice in the lower house for approval of re-election. But he added the process would be drawn out and may take until March.

Government leaders plan to put the amendment to a vote in a lower house committee on Jan 13 and to a first vote on the floor of the lower house two days later. The second vote would then, according to their forecast, take place on Jan 23.
Once in the Senate, where the government's support is more stable, the bill is unlikely to face major hurdles and Cardoso's sway over Congress will begin to grow, officials say.

"If re-election passes, the other reforms are going to gather a lot of speed," said Deputy Benito Gama, the government's leader in the Chamber of Deputies. "The prospect of the president being in power for six years is going to break down a lot of resistance in Congress."

Gama said, once re-election is resolved, priority treatment would be given to a civil service reform in the lower house while the Senate begins rebuilding a social security reform that was shorn of its most important points by rebellious deputies.
The reforms would be powerful tools in reducing Brazil's persistently sizable public sector deficit. But both have been stalled for months as the government concentrates on re-election.

Gama said a proposed reform to streamline and de-centralize Brazil's tax system, which has not begun committee-level talks, was on the agenda for 1997 but would require complex, and probably drawn-out, negotiations with states and municipalities.
The government would also seek to make swift progress on important legislation to regulate the opening up of the oil and telecommunications sectors, Gama said.
A final draft of a bill setting up a regulator for the petroleum industry would be presented to a lower house committee on Jan 8 and may be put to a vote in the chamber before the end of that month.
And one of the government's first tasks on returning in the New Year would be to appoint a deputy to take charge of a telecommunications privatization bill, Gama said.
"That could be explosive," said Brasilia University politics professor David Fleischer, adding that a bruising contest might muddy the waters for the government's re-election drive.

The government could also expect opposition within Congress to its plans to privatize mining giant Companhia Vale do Doce and the power sector while proposed changes to the electoral system might ruffle the feathers of parliamentarians seeking re-election in 1998, Fleischer said.
He said another potential pitfall for the Cardoso administration was a bill which would limit the president's powers to issue decrees.
But Fleischer said the probable approval of re-election would strengthen the government's hand in 1997.

"Even if it was rejected it would not be the end of the world because Cardoso's chosen successor would have the massive support of the government. But I'd say (re-election) has a 70 percent chance of passing," he said.
